verses.text: In the year that Tartan came to Ashdod, when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him, and he fought against Ashdod and took it;
at that time Yahweh spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, “Go, and loosen the sackcloth from off your waist, and take your shoes from off your feet.” He did so, walking naked and barefoot.
Yahweh said, “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and a wonder concerning Egypt and concerning Ethiopia,
so the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, and with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt.
They will be dismayed and confounded, because of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory.
The inhabitants of this coast land will say in that day, ‘Behold, this is our expectation, where we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria. And we, how will we escape?’”

footnotes.content: Tartan, the supreme military commander of Assyria, has captured Ashdod—a port city crucial to Philistine defense. The walls have fallen. Into this moment of military calamity, the Lord speaks to His prophet: not with comfort, but with a command that will seem madness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah obeys without hesitation or shame. He removes the sackcloth—already worn as a sign of mourning—and his shoes, and becomes naked and barefoot. Can you imagine? A prophet living this way through the streets. Obedience like this teaches us that the Lord's Word, spoken, is more worthy of our trust than our own comfort or reputation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three years. Not three days, three weeks—three full years Isaiah walks this humiliating path. The patience of this sign-act is staggering. Egypt and Ethiopia trust in their chariots and strength; the Lord is about to show what really lies beneath their pride. His servant's shameful body becomes the truth-teller.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What Isaiah's body has declared in advance, history will fulfill: Assyria's armies will drag Egypt's captives—leaders, children, elders—into exile, stripped and exposed. Their shame is the outcome of their rebellion against the God who rules nations. Isaiah's humiliation was love's warning. They did not listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ethiopia looked to Egypt as a protector; Egypt looked to its own brilliance. Both are confounded when the one they trusted proves helpless. In the end, all earthly might crumbles. Believers learn early: place no confidence in princes, no matter how storied their kingdoms. Jesus alone is our unshakeable hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo of this same question: 'If the strong cannot save the strong, how will we escape?' Every generation faces that moment—when earthly alliance fails and fear rises. The God of Isaiah spoke then; He still speaks now to those who listen: the Lord alone is refuge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
